newsitem.title: EGYPT: Arafat calls for more pressure on Israel.
newsitem.headline: Arafat calls for more pressure on Israel.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat urged the United States on Wednesday to put more pressure on Israel in order to rescue the Middle East peace process.

"It (the United States) must put pressure on the Israeli side, which is violating the agreements clearly and flagrantly," Arafat told reporters after a meeting with Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa.

Arafat held talks earlier in the day with President Hosni Mubarak. The two leaders consult often on the Middle East peace process, which has been stalled since Israel started building on March 18 a new 6,500-home Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem, which Israel occupied in 1967 and later annexed.
On March 21, a Palestinian militant opposed to peace killed himself and three Israelis in a Tel Aviv cafe bombing.
Israel claims all of Jerusalem as its undivided capital while Palestinians want the eastern part to be the capital of their future state.
Palestinians see Jewish settlement-building as pre-empting "final status" peace talks which have yet to resume since Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu took power last June.
Arafat said he asked Egypt to help muster international support to get the peace process on track and that one of the topics they discussed was holding an Arab summit.

"Netanyahu has brought the peace process to this situation, in which Israel is violating and breaking all that was agreed upon under U.S. President Bill Clinton's sponsorship in the White House in Washington," said Arafat, referring to a 1993 peace deal with Israel.

"Especially with regard to the Judaisation of Jerusalem, confiscation of land, building settlements, and destroying houses, not releasing detainees and others - 34 articles it has not implemented until now. We are not asking for more than what we have already agreed upon.
"America must know that the Palestinians will not at all accept wrongdoings," Arafat said.
Arafat last week met U.S. Middle East envoy Dennis Ross in the West Bank as part of U.S. efforts to broker peace, and Ross said there was a "very clear desire" to break the deadlock.
Arafat also sent a letter to Clinton complaining indirectly at Ross's performance and asking Clinton to personally step in to salvage the process, a Palestinian official had said.
The Palestinian leader said there was still hope "without doubt, in the fact that there is an international stand."
Moussa said the peace process was in a "major crisis" and urged all parties to rescue it.

"We are trying to find the best way to revive the peace process, which can never be revived alongside the policy of settlements and particularly things that affect Jerusalem and its status," Moussa added.
